stages.name: Information provision: strengths and weaknesses
stages.title: Information provision: strengths and weaknesses
stages.sub: Weigh up why giving people information can work well, and why it can still fail.

steps.q: A ban stops a good being sold at all, and a tax makes it more expensive to discourage buying it. Putting calorie labels on menus does neither of those things. Does it stop or price anyone out of ordering the meal?
steps.right: No, it leaves the decision to the customer
steps.wrong: Yes, it works the same as a ban or tax
steps.hint: A label only adds information. Does it remove the option or raise its price?

steps.q: Because the customer can still order the high-calorie meal if they want to, has their freedom to choose been taken away?
steps.right: No, their freedom to choose is kept
steps.wrong: Yes, their freedom to choose is removed
steps.hint: If the option is still there, is the choice still theirs?

steps.q: Ten years after cigarette packets first showed health warnings, most people now see smoking as harmful and unattractive without even reading the warning. Have people's underlying attitudes changed, or stayed the same?
steps.right: Their attitudes and norms have changed
steps.wrong: Their attitudes have stayed exactly the same
steps.hint: Think about whether the warning is still doing all the work, or whether beliefs themselves have moved.

steps.right: It keeps going for a long time
steps.wrong: It disappears as soon as the campaign stops

steps.q: The government runs adverts warning about the harms of sugary drinks. The drinks companies respond with their own adverts making sugary drinks look fun and harmless. Does the government's message still land as strongly?
steps.right: No, the firms' adverts weaken it
steps.wrong: Yes, the government's message always wins
